newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech PM's party seeks solidarity as vote looms.
newsitem.headline: Czech PM's party seeks solidarity as vote looms.

text.p: Leaders of Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's party called on coalition partners on Thursday to support their agreed emergency economic programme as internal rifts threatened to split the centre-right government.

In a statement answering reports that divisions were tearing apart Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS), the party's executive said it unanimiously backed the government ahead of a parliamentary vote of confidence expected next week.
"The leadership of ODS is in agreement that all of its members are committed to continue in the policies defined in the coalition statement announced (on May 28)," it said.

The ODS leadership also appeared to admonish the junior coalition partner, the Christian Democratic Union (KDU-CSL), which questioned aspects of the government's economic prgoramme, and the leadership of Klaus.
"The ODS leadership calls for the support of the coalition government and expresses its will to quickly and resolutely fulfil the programme to which the coalition has agreed."
The three-party coalition, after a sharp fall of the crown currency and plummeting popularity -- mainly that of the ODS, agreed to austerity measures and a cabinet reshuffle on May 28.

The plan, which included sharp budget cuts, public sector wage freezes and other belt-tightening steps meant to slow a dangerously high current account deficit, came with a statement that serious policy mistakes were made by the government.

The statement was a dramatic backdown for the monetarist economist Klaus, once regarded as the architect of one of post-Communist Europe's most successful economic transformations, and opened a fresh wave of criticism.

One of the most serious assaults came from Deputy Premier Josef Lux, the chairman of the centrist KDU-CSL, who claimed that Klaus intentionally withheld from ministers a fax written by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) warning earlier this year of a possible currency crisis.
Klaus denied that he withheld the IMF's warning from ministers, but his deputy party chairman, Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec, corroborated Lux's claim.
Zieleniec's statement sparked a rash of local media reports that an internal power struggle was blazing within the ODS.

The statement on Thursday appeared aimed at putting these reports to rest ahead of the confidence vote in the lower house where the coalition holds 100 of 200 seats and a simple majority is required for approval.
"(The ODS leadership) agreed that one of the key tasks is to overcome problems in mutual communication within the party and the coalition and renew the atmosphere of openness," the statement said.
